chapter_theme: The poet completes his praise of Rajamapuram, the city of Emangadam: banners, incense, gold swept away as refuse, guests fed from gold vessels, gifts to beggars, gods who watch unblinking, festivals without end, and wealth credited to the Jina's shrines; he then turns to the king and describes the moat, wall and four gate-towers, the king's bed-pavilion and his built pleasure-ground, whose pull already names the desire that will cost him his kingdom.

cast.role: king of Emangadam at Rajamapuram, Civakan's father

126.reading: The red-gold banners that rise from the rich city's tall buildings sway in turn, as if fanning the many-maned horses of the hot-rayed sun crossing the sky and cooling their blazing heat.
126.nuance: A fancy of cause (the banners wave in order to cool the sun's horses), the first of several in this run that make the city's height and wealth touch the heavens.

127.reading: The sweet incense smoke with which women dry the dampness of their jewelled breasts drifts round their earringed bright faces, so that each face looks like the great moon with its cool rays seen within a cloud.

128.reading: The red-gold chaplets children have thrown off, the gold garlands that have come loose and fallen, and the cool sandal paste rubbed from golden bodies are what the fragrant-garlanded women sweep aside as refuse.
128.nuance: The point is in the last line: in this city gold and sandal are what is swept away, so the refuse itself measures the wealth.

129.reading: On the soft floors washed with a scented wash, sandal paste is sprinkled in patterns, then pearls are scattered and golden flowers set down; in every quarter, the poet says, this is simply the way of wealth.
129.nuance: ஆரி in line 2 is a rare word; taking it as a pattern or design of the sprinkling is a guess.

130.reading: The smell of fried food and the smell of the precious agil smoke from the women's dark hair mix and choke, bringing tears to the eyes, so that the bright doves, it is said, have claimed the honeyed groves instead.
130.nuance: The sense of the doves' move (they leave the smoky houses for the groves outside) rests on reading உரிமை கொண்டன as 'took the groves as their own'; the verse leaves the subject's motion implicit.

131.reading: Using fragrant wood as fuel in silver hearths, the residents cook sweet ghee-rich food to the brim in gold vessels amid the smoke of musk and scent, and eat it together with their guests.
131.nuance: The only line in this catalogue of luxury that names a duty is the last: the food is eaten with guests (விருந்தொடும்). The verse states it as the city's custom, not as a precept.

132.reading: Standing in their tall white mansions, the beautiful women give betel, areca fruit with tender leaf, to their lion-strong men and set the day's fresh champak garlands on bright hair.
132.nuance: Whose hair (நகை முடி) receives the garland, the women's own or the men's, the verse does not settle.

133.reading: The women with painted, sword-like long eyes plough the saffron-smeared chests of their men with their warm breasts, sow garlands and sandal there with delight, and reap the joy of love.
133.nuance: The whole verse is a farming figure (உழுது, வித்தி, விளைப்பர): lovemaking as ploughing, sowing and harvest, so even pleasure is described in the language of the city's wealth.

134.reading: The flower-soft little feet of the women with fine dark hair, who wear anicham blossoms, shiver even on the heaped flowering cotton of their cloud-touching jewelled mansions.
134.nuance: The conceit of feet too tender for the softest things is the Kural's (1111, 1120 name anicham for it); here it is no lover's praise of one woman but a trait of a whole class of the city's women. Line 1 (குஞ்சி மேல் அனிச்ச மலர் கூட்டு உணும்) is hard: குஞ்சி is usually a man's hair, and கூட்டு உணும் may mean bees feeding on the blossoms; the reading of that line is not fixed.

135.reading: Those who enjoy only love on beds of fine cloth fragrant with smoke cannot tell the night watches from the day, so great is their passion, and the great city on earth has become like the golden world of the gods.
135.nuance: The comparison with heaven is praise, but the line about not knowing night from day is the same absorption the king will show in the verses that follow this run (198-201).

136.reading: The people of the golden city keep stores of gems spat out by serpents and pearls from the strong sea, and have taken on as their charge the giving of such things to those who come to beg.
136.nuance: புரவு பூண்டனர் makes giving a duty the people have bound themselves to, not occasional largesse.

137.reading: The gods do not blink even at night, as though, people say, they wished to watch the breast-wealth of women with jasmine-scented hair, the wealth of the great city and the wealth of its anklet-wearing rich.
137.nuance: A fancy built on the gods' epithet இமையார், 'the unblinking': the poet gives their nature a cause in the city's beauty.

138.reading: Drums and conches sound in the courtyards, and since festivals and weddings never cease the golden city is beyond praise; its noise is like the roar of the great sea being dug.
138.nuance: வேள்வு may mean a wedding or a sacrifice; with விழவு it most likely names the city's ceremonies in general.

139.reading: Because the sacred dwellings of the one with the moon-white triple umbrella stand everywhere, in every place, the wealth of the city never fails and it flourishes as if with the conch treasure.
139.nuance: The triple umbrella (முக்குடை) is the Jina's emblem, so this is the first verse of the run to give the city's wealth a religious cause; the verse does not say the Jina grants it, only that his shrines' presence is why it does not fail. திரு மாநகர் may instead mean that the whole city is his.

claims.claim: the presence of the Jina's shrines throughout a city keeps its prosperity from failing

140.reading: Such is Rajamapuram: a city whose wealth, like a grove of wish-granting trees hung with honey-dripping garlands, green cloth, gold blossoms, diamond and pearl strands and ambrosia, pours out its gifts to everyone.
140.nuance: The karpaga grove is the wish-tree of the gods' world; the verse names the city (இராசமா புரம்) only at the close of the long praise.

141.reading: The poet turns to the city's king, with his swift elephants, fierce spears, hot army, gracious sceptre, sky-high jewelled crown, rain-like giving hand, spotless renown, single command and white umbrella, and promises to tell a little of the goodness of the city.
141.nuance: The portrait is the standard catalogue of a just king; the gracious sceptre (ஐய கோல்) and single command are what the events later in this ilampakam (198-205) put in question.

142.reading: The broad moat, fed by water led across the land and descending through a decorated tunnel dug far underground, full of sharks fierce in their seizing, shone like an ornament the land had put on.

143.reading: The wall rose as if to split the sky's chest and see where it ends, adorned with clouds gathered about it; and since the heaven itself said it feared it, the wall seemed to beckon from there with the banner-hands on its crest.
143.nuance: நாகம் in line 2 may be heaven or the serpent; and who calls whom in lines 3-4 is unclear. The reading here, a fancy in which the wall's banners wave back at the frightened sky, is a guess.

144.reading: Four matching gate-towers, hung with triple strands of pearl garlands and with great jewelled doors, rise and shine like the four garlands on the jewelled crown of the gem-coloured god.
144.nuance: The simile uses மணிவணன், the gem-coloured god, a name of Tirumal; a Jain epic borrows a Vaishnava image for ornament without any claim. Line 3 (சத்தி நெற்றி சூட்டிய) is hard and the reading of it is not fixed.

145.reading: With women in pearl and sandal-decked breasts and fragrant garlands hanging in their hair coming in amorous joy to dance, the wealth of the city is like the wealth of red-eyed Indra's city; what more is there to say?
145.nuance: Lines 2 and 3 seem a foot or two short of this metre, so a word may be lost; the sense of who dances rests on the reading of those lines.

146.reading: The king's bed-chamber pavilion, with a silver bull elephant and soft cow elephant, a leaping stag of gleaming green gold and a pair of red-gold does, shines with green light; there the king dwells with desire burning within him.
146.nuance: Every figure in the pavilion is a mated pair, and the line about the king (உள்ளு காமம் உள் சுட) is the first time the run names the king's desire. It is stated, not judged, here.
146.event: The king lives in his bed-chamber pavilion, burning with desire.

147.reading: In the garden stand areca palms made of jewels: gem fronds like hair, clusters of round golden fruit of great gems and emerald, swelling spathes of white gold, and a swing of jewelled rope let down to sway.
147.nuance: The trees are artificial, made of metal and gems; the garden is a crafted thing.

148.reading: Soft heaps of millet, flashing waterfalls, blue lilies opening their eyes in jewelled pools beside the hill, and pairs of does standing to gaze: this is the lovely pleasure-ground that the burning desire of the king of the dark elephant longed for.
148.nuance: The king's park rebuilds the hill landscape of the old poems of love (millet, falls, pool lilies, deer) as a crafted scene. காம பூமி recurs in 189, where the royal couple are likened to the shining ones of the காம பூமி, the land of enjoyment.

149.reading: Where sweet koels mate, bees sleep in honey and others sing like bards, vengai trees drop gold, and the hill is wrapped in sandal, tall asoka, champak and naga trees give fragrance through the ages; to leave it would be to lose one's sweet life, and even to think of it makes the heart melt.
149.nuance: The last line turns description into attachment: the garden is a place one cannot part from without dying. The asoka (பிண்டி) is also the tree of the Jina, but nothing in the verse uses that.

links.note: The pavilion where the king dwells with desire burning in him is what a minister later names as the liquor of desire in which the king drowned and left the path of justice.
links.teaches: The lavish pavilion that reads as ornament is the poet's first, unjudged sign of the vice the minister will later blame for the king's ruin.

links.note: The garden one cannot leave without losing one's life anticipates the king's words that he cannot bear to part from Vijayai, for which he gives his rule to Kattiyangaran.
links.teaches: The garden's power to hold its owner is the same inability to part that later makes the king hand his kingdom to a minister.

links.note: The king introduced with a gracious sceptre and a single command is, some sixty verses later, the king who slips from guarding the land to cling to his queen.
links.teaches: The poet sets out the full catalogue of a just king's marks so that the reader can measure how far this king falls from them.

links.note: Both epics put a king with his beloved in a built pleasure-park of hills, falls, pools and deer.
links.teaches: The same crafted royal park is, in the Manimekalai, interrupted by news from the prison that turns the king to charity, and in the Cintamani the setting of a desire that costs the king his rule.

links.note: Kural 901 says men set on their wives miss the fine fruit and men of action do not want that desire; the epic shows a king whose rule is given up for it.
links.teaches: The Kural's flat warning becomes in the epic a seductive scene, so the reader is drawn into the very desire the couplet tells the man of action to refuse.

gains.a: The epic verse gets the moral frame its narrator withholds: the king's desire is the kind that a ruler is told to refuse.
gains.b: The couplet's unnamed 'fine fruit' is given concrete stakes: for a king the loss is his kingdom and his life.

links.note: The Kural's lover says anicham and swan's down are like nerunji to her feet; the epic has a whole city's women whose feet shiver on flowering cotton while they wear anicham.
links.teaches: A lover's private hyperbole about one woman's feet becomes in the epic a stock trait of a whole class of wealthy women, showing how the Kural's love conceits turned into description.

gains.a: The verse's strange shiver of feet on cotton is legible as a known conceit, so its point is degree of wealth, not novelty of image.
gains.b: The couplet's image is shown to have become public property, attached to a city's luxury rather than one lover's gaze.

links.note: Kural 81 says all of a household's keeping of goods is for caring for guests; the epic lists eating with guests as one item among the city's perfumes, gold and beds.
links.teaches: Where the Kural makes hospitality the purpose that justifies household wealth, the epic sets it inside a catalogue of pleasure, so the duty becomes one ornament of a city that will soon fall.

gains.a: The verse's single mention of guests is shown to carry the one moral justification of wealth in a run otherwise given to luxury.
gains.b: The couplet's rule is seen in a setting where wealth has outgrown the purpose the couplet gives it.

links.note: Tirumanthiram 518 says that if pujas in the First One's temple stop, kings suffer, the rains' bounty falls and theft spreads; the epic says the Jina's shrines everywhere keep the city's wealth from failing.
links.teaches: A Saiva manual and a Jain epic share the belief that shrines keep a land prosperous, but the Saiva verse ties it to rites that must not lapse while the Jain verse credits only the shrines' presence.

gains.a: The epic's brief claim is set in a wider Tamil belief tying a city's welfare to worship, so it reads as doctrine rather than mere praise.
gains.b: The Saiva warning is shown to be not only sectarian: a Jain text makes the same causal link without the threat of lapse.

source_issues: Verse 145: lines 2 and 3 are shorter than the other lines of this metre (141-149) and may have lost a word or a foot.
